The caliph asked him to release the deposed Buyid ruler and his companions; Tughril freed some prisoners but refused to let that one go, showing where authority now actually sat. He took the title King of the East and the West, and the Abbasid caliph kept his religious standing while Tughril's family held the real power behind it, a pattern that lasted for generations.

About six hundred people set out from Selma on 7 March 1965 to walk the fifty miles to Montgomery over the denial of Black voting rights. State troopers and mounted possemen met them at the Edmund Pettus Bridge and beat them back with clubs and tear gas; seventeen marchers needed hospital treatment, and organiser Amelia Boynton was photographed unconscious on the roadway.

Televised footage of that day, remembered as Bloody Sunday, pushed President Johnson to address Congress within the week, where he set Selma alongside Lexington and Appomattox. A third, protected march finally reached Montgomery on 25 March, and the Voting Rights Act became law that August, banning the literacy tests and other devices used to keep Black voters off the rolls.

Ottoman troops had garrisoned the Belgrade fortress since 1826, the last physical sign of the sultan's authority over Serbia, until an 1867 order withdrew them. Full independence still needed a war: Serbia fought the Ottomans twice between 1876 and 1878, the first conflicts of its modern history.

Those wars settled little on their own, and it took the great powers meeting in Berlin to make the outcome permanent. On 13 July 1878 the Treaty of Berlin recognised Serbia as fully independent, though it also handed neighbouring territory to Austria-Hungary rather than to Serbia itself.

Michael Servetus argued that the Trinity was a Greek philosophical addition with no basis in scripture and called infant baptism a device of the devil. He had said as much to John Calvin years earlier by post, and Calvin had already written to a friend that if Servetus ever came to Geneva, he would not leave it alive.

Servetus arrived anyway in 1553 and was arrested. Calvin pressed the council toward a death sentence, asking only that Servetus be beheaded rather than burned; the council, led by Ami Perrin, chose burning instead, and Servetus died at the stake on 27 October 1553, still refusing to recant.

Ohio senator John Sherman wrote the bill that carries his name, and Congress passed it almost without dissent: 52 to 1 in the Senate, unanimous in the House. President Benjamin Harrison signed it on 2 July 1890, giving the federal government its first statute against monopolies and the cartels then known as trusts.

For its first years the law mostly disappointed the people who had pushed for it. Courts moved slowly, and in 1894 the Supreme Court ruled a sugar-refining monopoly outside its reach entirely, reading the statute narrowly. It took until 1904 and the breakup of Northern Securities Company for a case to show the act could actually dissolve a trust, fourteen years after it was signed.

Outside a church in Palermo on Easter Monday, 1282, a French sergeant assaulted a young Sicilian woman and her husband stabbed him dead. As the bells rang for vespers, the crowd turned on the French garrison around them, and by nightfall thousands of French men and women in the city were dead, reportedly picked out by demanding suspects say the word ciciri, a sound French speakers could not manage.

The killing spread across the island within weeks, ending Charles of Anjou's rule there almost overnight. The rebels then invited Peter III of Aragon, married to a Hohenstaufen heir, to take the crown, turning a single riot into a war between Aragon and the Angevins that dragged on for two decades.

Zhang Qian set out around 138 BCE to find allies against the Xiongnu and was captured by them instead, spending roughly thirteen years among his captors before he finally reached the lands he had been sent to. He came home having found no ally, but with detailed reports of kingdoms in Central Asia that China had never known existed.

Emperor Wu sent embassies west on the strength of those reports, some several hundred strong, carrying Chinese silk out and bringing horses and unfamiliar goods back. Zhang Qian's journey did not create trade between China and the Mediterranean by itself, but it is the point at which the routes stopped being rumour and started being mapped.

Zhang Qian was not sent to open a trade route. In 138 BC Emperor Wu dispatched him west to find military allies against the Xiongnu, the nomadic power blocking Han China from the lands beyond it. The Xiongnu caught him almost immediately and held him for thirteen years, during which he married and had children among his captors.

He escaped, reached Central Asia, and found the alliance he sought was no longer wanted, the people he had been sent to court having settled into peace. What he brought home instead, in 125 BC, was detailed knowledge of wealthy kingdoms to the west. Later missions to those kingdoms turned that intelligence into the caravan routes historians later named for silk.

Singapore had joined the Federation of Malaysia only in 1963, and the merger did not settle much. Trade disputes, disagreements over race-based policy and communal riots in 1964 left the two governments barely on speaking terms within two years of union.

Secret talks between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore produced a separation agreement, and on 9 August 1965 the Malaysian Parliament voted 126 to 0 to let Singapore go. Lee Kuan Yew, who had campaigned for merger, became prime minister of a country he had not sought, with no natural resources and a population he once doubted could survive alone.

More than a thousand economists signed a joint letter begging Herbert Hoover to veto the bill before he signed it on 17 June 1930. Henry Ford reportedly called it economic stupidity in person, and the head of J.P. Morgan later said he had nearly gone down on his knees to plead with Hoover against it.

Named for Senator Reed Smoot and Representative Willis Hawley, the act raised duties on thousands of imported goods. Canada, France, Italy and half a dozen other trading partners answered with tariffs of their own; American exports to the countries that retaliated fell by roughly a third, and world trade as a whole collapsed by around two thirds over the next four years.

Edward Snowden spent months exchanging encrypted messages with a documentary filmmaker and a journalist before flying to Hong Kong in May 2013 to hand over the files in person. The first story ran in The Guardian on 5 June, describing a program called PRISM that gave the National Security Agency direct access to user data held by Microsoft, Google, Facebook, Apple and several other major companies.

Once his identity became public days later, Snowden fled toward Latin America but got no further than Moscow, where a cancelled passport left him stranded at the airport for weeks before Russia granted him asylum. He remains there today, having become a Russian citizen in 2022, while the journalists who reported his leaks shared a Pulitzer Prize.

Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act on 14 August 1935, creating a federal pension funded by a payroll tax on current workers rather than by savings each person had set aside. Alongside old-age benefits it set up state-run unemployment insurance and aid for families headed by a single mother, the first time the federal government had underwritten either.

The original law left large groups out: farm labourers, domestic servants and most government employees were not covered, a gap that fell hardest on Black workers in the rural South, where a majority of them worked in excluded jobs. Congress extended coverage to most of these groups only in later decades.

Rome's Italian allies supplied soldiers for its wars without receiving Roman citizenship or a vote in Roman assemblies. In 91 BC, after the reformer Marcus Livius Drusus was assassinated and his proposals to extend citizenship collapsed with him, several allied peoples, including the Marsi and Samnites, rose in revolt rather than wait any longer.

The fighting was costly enough that Rome, mid war, began offering citizenship to communities willing to lay down arms, hoping to split the rebellion rather than defeat it outright. It worked: citizenship was extended across Italy over the following years, though a bitter argument over which of Rome's voting tribes the new citizens would join outlasted the war itself and fed directly into the political violence of the following decade.

Socrates was convicted by a jury of 501 Athenians, and the vote was close: 280 for guilty, 221 for acquittal. The charges were impiety and corrupting the young; among his former students had been Alcibiades and Critias, men many Athenians blamed for the city's recent slide into war and oligarchy.

Offered a chance to propose his own lesser sentence, Socrates reportedly suggested the city award him free meals for life, which only angered the jury further. He drank the hemlock himself at about seventy, and Plato later wrote that the poison crept upward from his legs while his mind stayed clear to the end.

A watchtower in Gansu preserved a letter, dated to 313, from a Sogdian trader warning colleagues that the route east had gone bad. It is one of the earliest direct records of a merchant network that by the 6th century ran the full 1,500 miles from Sogdiana to China, rather than handing goods off between oasis towns.

Their language became the trade tongue of Central Asia and the court language of the Turkic Khaganate that protected their caravans. Along with silk and metalwork, Sogdian traders carried Zoroastrianism, Manichaeism and Buddhism eastward, and Nestorian Christianity followed the same roads into China.

Other Central Asian traders were sometimes simply called by the Sogdians' name, a measure of how thoroughly Sogdian colonies had come to run Silk Road commerce by 600. Their settlements stretched from their Central Asian homeland to garrison towns deep inside China, each one staffed by merchants who spoke the local language alongside their own.

That fluency, not just goods, was the real export. Sogdian became the working language of trade and diplomacy across the region, used at the Turkic khagan's court as readily as in market towns, letting Sogdian intermediaries broker deals between Chinese, Turkic and Persian parties who otherwise shared no common tongue.

By the 6th century Samarkand sat behind four rows of walls and four gates, an organised city rather than a caravan stop, positioned exactly where routes from China, Persia and the lands beyond met. That position, more than any single ruler, made it the Sogdian civilisation's principal centre.

Around 550 the Western Turkic Khaganate took the region from the Hephthalites and struck marriage alliances with Samarkand's rulers, giving merchants there the political cover to keep trading through a change of overlords. Sogdian traders based in the city carried goods, and their own language, along the routes their city commanded.

The strike began over the firing of a crane operator, Anna Walentynowicz, at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk. By the end of August 1980 the government had agreed to let the workers organise outside party control, and on 17 September delegates from across Poland registered Solidarity as a single national union, with Lech Walesa as its chairman.

Membership reached nearly ten million within a year, roughly a third of Poland's working population. Martial law shut the union down in December 1981 and jailed its leaders, but it survived underground until round table talks with the government in 1989 led to elections that ended communist rule in Poland.

Zhao Kuangyin did not seize power through open rebellion but through a staged mutiny. His own soldiers, the story goes, draped a yellow robe over him at Chenqiao in 960 and refused to march further under anyone else, forcing the boy emperor of the Later Zhou to abdicate in his favour. He took the name Taizu and spent sixteen years subduing the remaining kingdoms to reunify China.

The dynasty he founded is remembered less for its army than for what it printed, financed and built. Song China issued the world's first paper banknotes, developed movable type printing, fitted ships with a compass for true north, and fielded gunpowder weapons including fire lances, all inside a state that also recruited its officials through competitive written examinations.

A special convention met in Columbia on 17 December 1860, then moved to Charleston to finish its work. On 20 December delegates voted 169 to nothing to dissolve the state's union with the rest of the United States, the first such vote by any state.

Four days later the convention issued a declaration explaining itself, and it did not equivocate: it named the election of a president hostile to slavery and northern refusal to return escaped slaves as its grievances. Six more states left within weeks, and by February a rival confederacy had formed around them.

The South Sea Company existed to manage government debt, not to trade much, but its directors spread extravagant rumours of riches from Spanish American markets it barely touched. Shares that traded at £128 in January 1720 hit £1,000 by August, bought on credit the company itself was lending out.

The scheme could not survive selling pressure, and by autumn the price had fallen back below £150, wiping out thousands of investors. A parliamentary inquiry found fraud reaching into the cabinet: the chancellor of the exchequer went to prison, two ministers died in disgrace, and Robert Walpole oversaw the confiscation of most of the company directors' wealth to repay victims.

Mikhail Gorbachev had called the occupation a bleeding wound as early as 1986, and by mid-1987 announced the army would leave entirely. The Geneva Accords, signed by Afghanistan, Pakistan, the United States and the Soviet Union in April 1988, set the terms and timetable for a pullout that had taken years of quiet argument inside the Kremlin to agree.

Soviet troops began leaving under that timetable and the last column crossed the Amu Darya into the Uzbek SSR on 15 February 1989, ending a war that had drained the Soviet military, economy and political standing for nine years. The communist government left behind in Kabul fought on alone until 1992, when Moscow's financial support stopped following the Soviet Union's own collapse.

Francisco Franco died on 20 November 1975 after ruling Spain for thirty six years, and two days later Juan Carlos was sworn in as king under the very laws Franco had designed to keep the dictatorship intact after him. Instead the new king backed reform, appointing Adolfo Suarez as prime minister in 1976 to dismantle the system from within.

Suarez legalised the previously outlawed Communist Party in April 1977, a step his own cabinet warned could provoke the army, and held Spain's first free elections that June. A new constitution followed in a December 1978 referendum, and the transition survived its sternest test in 1981 when the king publicly opposed an attempted military coup.

Earlier traders had crept along the coast from the Red Sea to India, trading through middlemen at ports like Aden and taking months to do it. Once Roman sailors worked out how to ride the summer monsoon straight across the open Arabian Sea and the winter monsoon back, a return voyage to India's Malabar coast became a single season's trip instead of a hazard-strewn crawl.

The geographer Strabo reported that around 120 ships a year sailed for India from the Egyptian port of Myos Hormos under Augustus, against a handful under the Ptolemies before Rome took Egypt. Pepper, cinnamon and other spices flowed west in such volume that pepper warehouses were later built in Rome itself, while Roman gold coin flowed east in exchange, turning up in hoards across southern India.

Parliament passed the Stamp Act on 22 March 1765, requiring that colonial newspapers, legal documents, playing cards and even dice carry an embossed revenue stamp bought with British coin rather than colonial paper money. It took effect that November, the first direct tax Britain had levied on the American colonies rather than a duty on trade.

Colonial assemblies petitioned against it, and delegates from nine colonies met as the Stamp Act Congress that October. Mobs intimidated the appointed stamp distributors into resigning, so the tax was never effectively collected anywhere. Parliament repealed it on 18 March 1766, but the argument it provoked, that taxation required representation, did not go away with it.

John D. Rockefeller incorporated Standard Oil in Ohio in 1870 with a million dollars of capital, alongside his brother William, chemist Samuel Andrews and four other partners. What set the firm apart at first was not size but thrift: while rival refiners dumped the heavy waste from kerosene production, Rockefeller found buyers for it.

A railroad deal in 1868 had already given his earlier company a shipping rate far below what competitors paid, and he used the margin to undercut them on price and then buy them out. By 1904 Standard controlled roughly nine tenths of American oil refining.

Talks over cutting long-range nuclear arsenals had dragged on for nearly a decade, stalled repeatedly by disputes over verification and which weapons to count. George H. W. Bush and Mikhail Gorbachev finally signed the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty in Moscow on 31 July 1991, the first agreement to cut rather than merely cap the two superpowers' strategic arsenals.

The treaty capped each side at 6,000 deployed warheads and 1,600 intercontinental missiles and bombers combined. The Soviet Union collapsed five months later, and ratification had to be renegotiated among Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan before the reductions it set out were actually carried through.

Before 1710, printing rights in England belonged to the Stationers' Company, a guild that had held a near-permanent monopoly on what could legally be published since the previous century. The Statute of Anne broke that hold by putting copyright into law for the first time and, crucially, giving it to authors rather than the printers who set their type.

The term was modest by later standards: fourteen years from publication, with a second fourteen-year renewal if the author was still alive when it expired. Works already in print got twenty-one years. Once the clock ran out, the text became free for anyone to print, a deliberate limit that later copyright law kept extending but never dropped.

Before 1931, an act passed at Westminster could bind Canada, Australia or the other dominions whether or not their own parliaments agreed to it. The Statute of Westminster ended that: it barred any future UK law from applying to a dominion unless that dominion had asked for it, turning a legal hierarchy into a group of equals bound only by shared allegiance to the Crown.

Canada, the Irish Free State and South Africa took the statute's effect immediately in 1931; Australia, New Zealand and Newfoundland delayed formal adoption for years afterward. It followed directly from the Balfour Declaration of 1926, in which Britain and the dominions had already agreed, in principle, that none stood subordinate to another.

Sudan had been ruled since 1899 as an Anglo-Egyptian condominium, nominally shared between Cairo and London but administered in practice much like a British colony. That arrangement began to unravel after Egypt's 1952 revolution, whose leaders, including the half-Sudanese Muhammad Naguib, pressed for British withdrawal from both Egypt and Sudan.

Sudan became fully independent on 1 January 1956, ending both British and Egyptian authority at once rather than transferring power from one to the other. A parliamentary government took office in Khartoum, though the new state inherited a divide between the Arab-majority north and the south that would erupt into civil war within months.

Sulla had been given command against Mithridates in the east, then had it stripped from him by a political manoeuvre in Rome favouring his rival Marius. Rather than accept it, in 88 BC he marched his legions on Rome itself, the first Roman general to lead an army against the city. He won that round, left for his eastern campaign, and returned in 83 BC to fight a second civil war against Marius's allies.

Sulla had himself made dictator in 82 BC, not as a temporary emergency office in the old sense but with no fixed term, and published proscription lists naming enemies who could be killed for a reward. He resigned the dictatorship after roughly two years and retired from politics, but the precedent he set, that a general's personal army could decide who ruled Rome, outlived him.

The document dated 1291 says nothing about crossbows or apples. It is a defensive pact among three valley communities, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, promising mutual help and a peaceful way to settle disputes among themselves, mainly to keep their mountain trade routes free of outside interference. The famous oath on the Rutli meadow, tied to the William Tell story, is a later tradition, dated by a sixteenth century chronicler to 1307.

The three Forest communities fought off a Habsburg army in 1315 and pledged, from then on, not to make outside alliances without each other's consent. Other valleys and cities joined over the following centuries, and the loose alliance that grew from this original charter became modern Switzerland, which still marks 1291 as its founding date.

Mark Sykes and Francois Georges-Picot spent the winter of 1915 into 1916 drawing a line across a map of Ottoman territory neither man had much reason to think he owned yet. Britain took the southern strip running toward the Gulf and a claim on Mediterranean ports; France took the north, covering Syria, Lebanon and what is now southeastern Turkey; Palestine was set aside for international control.

None of this squared with promises Britain had separately made to Arab leaders about postwar independence. The arrangement stayed secret until the new Bolshevik government, hostile to the old tsarist alliances, published the text in Moscow in November 1917; the Manchester Guardian reprinted it days later, and Arab trust in British assurances never fully recovered.

Afghanistan's capital had already endured four years of factional shelling among former anti-Soviet militias when Taliban fighters entered Kabul on 27 September 1996. Former president Mohammad Najibullah had been sheltering inside the UN compound since his government fell in 1992; the Taliban dragged him out, tortured him and killed him the same night, then hung his body from a traffic post.

The new authorities announced the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan and imposed a strict reading of sharia within days: women were barred from most work and schooling, television and music were banned, and men were required to grow beards. The takeover ended the civil war among the mujahideen factions but replaced it with a new and isolated government.

Li Yuan did not plan a dynasty so much as survive one collapsing around him. As a Sui official and cousin of the reigning emperor, he watched Sui rule disintegrate into revolt, and in 618, after Emperor Yang was murdered by his own officers, Li Yuan declared himself emperor rather than wait to be swept away with the regime he had served.

His rebellion had an unusual figure at its edge: his daughter, Princess Pingyang, who raised and personally commanded her own troops during the fighting. Once established, the dynasty's second ruler, Li Shimin, pushed Tang territory past the old Han borders and drew up a legal code that Chinese dynasties kept copying for centuries.

On the morning of 20 June 1789, deputies of France's Third Estate arrived at their usual hall to find the doors locked and guarded on the king's order. Fearing they were about to be dispersed by force, they followed a suggestion from Joseph-Ignace Guillotin and moved to a nearby indoor tennis court at Versailles instead.

There, led by the astronomer Jean Sylvain Bailly, 576 of the 577 deputies present swore not to separate until France had a written constitution. Only Joseph Martin-Dauch refused, saying he would obey no decision but the king's. The oath turned a locked-out assembly into a body claiming to speak for the nation.

The Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States signed the treaty in Moscow on 5 August 1963, less than a year after the Cuban Missile Crisis had shown how close the two superpowers could come to disaster. It took effect that October and well over a hundred further countries eventually joined it.

Negotiators had originally hoped for a complete ban but gave up on covering underground tests, since verifying them without intrusive inspections proved technically hard and politically unwelcome to Moscow. What the treaty did stop was atmospheric, underwater and space detonations, ending the practice of venting fallout directly into the air that people breathed.

A two-thirds Senate majority for annexation could not be found, so President Tyler took a shortcut: a joint resolution needing only a simple majority in each house. Congress passed it in March 1845, and Texans ratified it that autumn, ending nine years as an independent republic that Mexico had never recognised.

Mexico had warned that annexation meant war, and it did. The Mexican minister broke relations before the ink was dry, and fighting began the following spring over the disputed border with Mexico. In Washington the deeper argument was slavery: adding one more slave state threatened the careful balance Congress had held in the Senate for a generation.

By 1834 around 30,000 Anglo-American settlers in Texas outnumbered Mexican-born residents there by roughly four to one, and Santa Anna's decision to scrap Mexico's 1824 constitution and rule by central decree cost Texas the local autonomy that had made the imbalance tolerable. Fighting broke out at Gonzales in October 1835 over a single cannon the Mexican army wanted back.

The Alamo fell on 6 March 1836 after a thirteen day siege, with almost every defender killed, William Travis and Davy Crockett among them. Six weeks later Sam Houston's army caught Santa Anna's force by surprise at San Jacinto, routed it in under twenty minutes, and captured the general himself, who bought his life by ordering Mexican troops out of Texas.

A winter of strikes across public services, remembered as the Winter of Discontent, had left the Labour government of James Callaghan looking unable to govern. Thatcher, who had led the Conservative Party since beating Edward Heath for it in 1975, won the general election of 4 May 1979 and took office that day as the first woman to hold the post in Britain.

She arrived promising to curb the power of trade unions, sell off state-owned industries and pull the state back from managing the economy directly, a break from the postwar consensus both parties had largely shared. Unemployment and industrial disputes marked her early years in office before the policies associated with her name became shorthand for the decade, a term applied to her governments rather than one she coined herself.

Theodoric took Italy from a man he had been sent to remove. Emperor Zeno ordered him against Odoacer, the general who had deposed Rome's last western emperor, and after years of campaigning the two agreed in February 493 to rule Italy jointly.

The peace lasted ten days. At a banquet marking Theodoric's entry into Ravenna, he raised a toast, then drew his sword and cut Odoacer down himself. He went on to settle around forty thousand Ostrogoths across Italy and rule it for over three decades, keeping Roman administration largely intact under Gothic kings.

Nobody had organised Roman law in over a century when Theodosius II ordered the job done in 429. Imperial rulings since Constantine's reign, more than 2,500 of them scattered across a hundred years of edicts, letters and rescripts, were gathered, sorted by subject and stripped of anything obsolete or contradictory.

The finished code was published in February 438 and took effect across both halves of the empire, east and west, on the first day of the following January, with Valentinian III agreeing to enforce it in Ravenna as well as Constantinople. It gave later compilers, including Justinian a century afterward, a model to build on rather than start from scratch.

On 11 December 220, the last Han emperor, Xian, abdicated to Cao Pi, who had inherited his father Cao Cao's grip on the north and now took the throne himself. Xian had reigned for three decades as a figurehead while warlords fought over the empire behind him; he was allowed to live out his life with a noble title rather than executed.

Within a year two rivals answered by declaring their own emperors: Liu Bei in the southwest and, later, Sun Quan in the Yangtze south. The three courts, Wei, Shu and Wu, fought and allied in shifting combinations for six decades until Jin absorbed the last of them in 280. Storytellers turned the period into China's most retold cycle of war and betrayal long before any of it was called history.

Roman law had long capped how much public land any one citizen could hold, a limit the wealthy had simply ignored for generations. As tribune in 133 BC, Tiberius Gracchus revived the cap and proposed redistributing the surplus to landless citizens, bypassing the Senate by taking the bill straight to the popular assembly.

Seeking re-election to push the law through, Tiberius was confronted at a crowded voting site by a mob led by his own cousin, Scipio Nasica. He and many supporters were beaten to death with clubs and stones, and their bodies were thrown into the Tiber rather than buried. His land commission survived him and distributed over a million iugera of land, but the killing showed that Roman political disputes could now be settled with violence.

Before settling on a name, Briton Hadden and Henry Luce nearly called their new venture Facts, to signal how brief it would be. The first issue reached newsstands on 3 March 1923 under the title they chose instead, with the slogan Take Time, It's Brief printed under the masthead.

Its formula was not more news but less: a week's events condensed into short, brisk items organised by section, written in a clipped, opinionated house voice. Covers put a single face on the front rather than a headline event, a choice that made the magazine's founders, still in their twenties, the template for a century of American newsweeklies.

Tiwanaku had been growing in the Titicaca basin since roughly 200, but it reached its peak of influence between 500 and 600, when its reach stretched well beyond the altiplano into Peru's Moquegua valley, where settlements built in Tiwanaku's own architectural style appear far from the capital.

The state relied less on conquest than on elite gift-giving and llama caravan networks, images of loaded pack animals turn up on portable objects traded across the region. Its capital near Lake Titicaca grew to hold over ten thousand people and produced the massive stonework of the Akapana platform and the Gateway of the Sun.

The largest of the Tarim Basin's oasis states, Kucha, is thought to have held some eighty thousand people, ringed by desert on every side and kept alive by irrigation drawn from the surrounding mountains. Its rulers spoke a language related to no neighbour, an Indo-European tongue that had somehow ended up isolated deep in Central Asia.

That language survives only in manuscripts, thousands of them, written centuries after these kingdoms' peak using an alphabet borrowed from Indian Brahmi script. The oases themselves existed to keep caravans moving between China and the west, and it was through them that Buddhism, carried along the same roads, first reached Chinese-speaking lands in force.

Tokugawa Ieyasu had already won the decisive battle three years earlier at Sekigahara, ending a century of civil war among Japan's regional lords. In 1603 he took the title of shogun and ruled from Edo Castle, in what is now Tokyo, leaving the emperor in Kyoto as a figurehead while real authority sat with him and the daimyo who answered to him.

The isolation the shogunate became known for took decades to close in fully. Ieyasu banned Catholicism outright in 1614, and by 1635 his successors barred Japanese subjects from leaving the country and shut the ports to everyone but China, Korea and the Dutch, a policy that held with little change until the mid-1800s.

Toledo's own Muslim ruler, al-Qadir, asked Alfonso VI of Castile for help putting down an uprising against him. Alfonso obliged, then kept the city for himself, and after a long siege it fell on 25 May 1085. Al-Qadir was compensated with a lesser throne in Valencia, where he was killed a few years later.

Alfonso first let Toledo's Muslims keep their great mosque and property, and even took the title emperor of the two religions. The concession did not last: while he was away, the newly appointed archbishop, Bernard of Sedirac, seized the mosque with the queen's backing and consecrated it as a cathedral.

Nerva, an elderly senator installed as emperor after Domitian's assassination, had no son and needed a successor the army would accept. In 97 he adopted Trajan, a general commanding legions on the Rhine, and when Nerva died in January 98 Trajan succeeded him without contest, the first emperor born outside Italy, in the Roman province of Hispania.

Trajan spent much of his reign on campaign rather than in Rome, annexing Dacia and, late in his rule, pushing into Mesopotamia against the Parthians. Under him the empire reached its largest territorial extent, stretching from Britain to the Persian Gulf, though the eastern gains proved impossible for his successor to hold and were abandoned soon after Trajan's death in 117.

Camels had crossed the Sahara since the 3rd century, but regular caravan routes only formed once Islam began spreading through West Africa in the 7th and 8th centuries, giving traders on both sides a shared law and language to trade under. Gold moved north from Wangara toward Sijilmasa in Morocco, then on to Mediterranean ports.

Salt moved the other way, and at Timbuktu it changed hands for close to its weight in gold. Timbuktu, Gao and Djenne grew rich as staging posts on that exchange, and the trade in gold, salt, slaves and kola nuts along the Taghaza and Walata trails ran at that scale into the early 17th century.

Britain handed the French fortress of Louisbourg back to France in exchange for Madras, a trading post in India that a French fleet had captured three years earlier. British and American colonists who had bled to take Louisbourg were furious to see a European negotiator swap it for a foothold on another continent entirely.

Every major power signed the 1748 settlement and almost none of them liked it. Maria Theresa got her succession as Habsburg ruler confirmed but resented losing Silesia to Prussia in the bargain, Spain thought its gains too small, and France's own public called the peace as bad as the war it ended. Most parties treated it as a pause rather than a resolution, and fighting resumed within eight years.

Castile and Portugal signed the Treaty of Alcacovas on 4 September 1479 to end a war neither side had clearly won. Castile's forces, backed by Ferdinand and Isabella, had the upper hand on land, while Portugal's fleets controlled the sea, so the settlement split the difference: the rival claimant to Castile's throne renounced her claim, and a royal marriage sealed the peace.

Buried in the same treaty was a division of the Atlantic that would matter more than the war itself. Castile kept the Canary Islands, while Portugal secured Madeira, the Azores, Cape Verde and the West African coast, along with exclusive rights to sail and trade anywhere in the ocean south of the Canaries. Thirteen years before Columbus sailed, the two crowns had already agreed how to carve up an Atlantic neither had explored.

The 1667 settlement between England and the Dutch Republic was less a negotiation than a bookkeeping exercise. The two sides agreed on uti possidetis, a principle that each kept whatever it currently held on the ground, with an effective date set for 20 May of that year. It was a quick way to end a war neither side was winning outright.

Under that rule, the Dutch kept Suriname, a South American sugar colony, and the nutmeg island of Run, while England kept New Netherland, seized from the Dutch two years earlier and already renamed New York after the king's brother. At the time, the nutmeg island looked like the better prize.

Robert Cecil led the English delegation that met Spanish and Habsburg envoys in London in 1604, closing a war that had run since 1585 without either side ever forcing a decision. Elizabeth I, who had backed the fight for two decades, had died the year before, and her successor James I had little appetite for continuing it.

The peace restored the position each side had held before the fighting started. Spain accepted James's Protestant crown and dropped any plan to restore Catholicism in England; England, in turn, stopped funding the Dutch rebels and English ships stopped raiding Spanish shipping in the Atlantic. Spain also agreed to end its military involvement in Ireland.

Francis I had been captured at the Battle of Pavia in 1525 and held in Spain for almost a year before he would agree to terms. The treaty he signed in Madrid in January 1526 gave up his claims to Burgundy, Flanders, Artois and Italy, and left his two young sons behind as hostages against his word.

His word did not last long. Within weeks of returning to France he repudiated the treaty, arguing he had signed it only under duress as a prisoner, and formed the League of Cognac against Charles V instead. Burgundy stayed French; the war over Italy dragged on for years more.

The agreement was signed aboard the British warship HMS Cornwallis, anchored off Nanjing, on 29 August 1842. It closed the First Opium War, fought after Chinese officials destroyed British-owned opium stocks at Canton, and it was written entirely on British terms.

Beyond handing over Hong Kong, the treaty forced open four more ports, Xiamen, Fuzhou, Ningbo and Shanghai, to foreign trade, and required 27 million silver dollars, covering the destroyed opium, the 1841 ransom of Canton, merchant debts and British war costs. It was the first of what China would later call the unequal treaties, a term that stuck to the whole series that followed it.

Nijmegen was not one treaty but a sequence signed by exhausted parties between 1678 and 1679, closing out the Franco-Dutch War: France and the Dutch Republic first, then France and Spain, then settlements with Brandenburg, Sweden, Denmark and the Holy Roman Empire trailing behind. Louis XIV negotiated separately with each so that no ally could hold up his terms with the others.

France gave up Maastricht and the Principality of Orange to William of Orange, but took Franche-Comte outright from Spain along with a run of Flanders and Hainaut towns, including Ypres, Cassel and Valenciennes. The new French border it left behind sat close to where the modern frontier with Belgium still runs.

Charlemagne had already been crowned emperor by the Pope in Rome in 800, a title Constantinople refused to recognise since it considered itself the sole heir of the Roman Caesars. Twelve years of intermittent war and negotiation over Venice and the Dalmatian coast followed before Byzantine envoys came to Aachen in 812 with an offer: Michael I would call Charlemagne emperor if Charlemagne gave up his claims in the Adriatic.

Michael's recognition still withheld the phrase that mattered most to Byzantine pride, emperor of the Romans, since Constantinople kept that title for itself alone. Even a partial acknowledgement was new: a Western ruler now held an imperial title a Byzantine emperor had agreed to use, splitting in practice what neither side would concede in words.

Under the treaty signed near Chartres in 1360, Edward III kept vast southwestern French lands, including Gascony, Poitou and Calais, and was to hold them outright rather than as a vassal owing homage to the French crown. In exchange he gave up his claim to the French throne itself, the demand that had opened the Hundred Years' War over two decades earlier.

The captured King John II's freedom came at a price fixed at three million ecus, with release allowed once a third was paid; his own sons and a roll of nobles and town representatives were handed over as hostages against the rest. The settlement bought only nine years of peace before fighting resumed.

France signed away the war it had started. The treaty, concluded at Frankfurt on 10 May 1871, closed the Franco-Prussian War by handing Germany most of Alsace and a large slice of Lorraine, some 1,600 towns and villages in all.

Residents of the ceded territory had until October 1872 to choose French citizenship and leave, or stay and become German subjects. France also owed five billion francs in reparations, which it paid off faster than the five years allowed, and German troops withdrew from French soil by September 1873.

Neither side got what it had gone to war for. The American delegation, led by John Quincy Adams and Henry Clay, wanted an end to British impressment of sailors; the treaty signed at Ghent on 24 December 1814 does not mention it. Both sides simply agreed to give back what they had taken and return to the borders that existed before the fighting began.

News travelled by ship, so nobody at Ghent could stop what came next. Andrew Jackson's forces crushed a British assault on New Orleans on 8 January 1815, two weeks after the peace was signed and long before word of it crossed the Atlantic, leaving Americans to celebrate a victory in a war that had already ended on paper.

Twenty one years of war between Russia and Sweden ended at a small Finnish town on 10 September 1721. Russia kept Ingria, Estonia, Livonia and part of Karelia, land it had fought two decades to hold, and paid Sweden two million silver riksdaler in compensation for the loss.

Sweden kept most of Finland but lost its place among the great powers, entering what its own historians call the Age of Liberty, a period of weakened royal authority at home. Russia, by contrast, emerged from Nystad with a Baltic coastline and the standing of a new European empire.

Bohdan Khmelnytsky had led a Cossack revolt against Polish rule for six years and needed a stronger patron than his own exhausted army. In January 1654 at Pereyaslav he swore allegiance to Tsar Alexis of Russia, whose envoy Vasily Buturlin promised military protection in return, along with a degree of Cossack self-rule under the Kyiv church.

What exactly changed hands is still argued over. Some historians read it as Cossack incorporation into Moscow, others as an autonomous protectorate, others as a personal union between two states. Soviet writers later called it the unification of brotherly peoples; Ukrainian nationalist historians call it the moment self-government began slipping away.

By 1714 both sides had run out of reasons to keep fighting. France's Claude Louis Hector de Villars and Austria's Prince Eugene of Savoy, generals who had fought each other for years, sat down at Rastatt to finish what the Treaty of Utrecht had left unresolved between their two courts.

Austria came away the winner. It took Naples, Milan and Sardinia from Spanish Italy, added the former Spanish Netherlands, and picked up Freiburg and small border districts from France. The Habsburgs now held more territory than at any point since Charles V had divided his inheritance in 1556.

Li Hongzhang, representing a Qing government that had just lost its fleet and its northern armies, negotiated the terms in the Japanese port town for which the treaty is named, signing alongside Ito Hirobumi in April 1895. Beyond Taiwan and Korean independence, China ceded the Liaodong Peninsula and agreed to pay 200 million taels of silver over seven years, and opened four more cities to Japanese trade.

The settlement did not hold as written. Six days after signing, Russia, France and Germany jointly pressed Japan to give up Liaodong, fearing it would threaten Russian ambitions at Port Arthur. Japan complied that November in exchange for a further 30 million taels, but the forced retreat left a lasting sense of grievance in Tokyo that fed directly into the Russo-Japanese War a decade later.

Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and John Jay signed for the United States on 3 September 1783, at a house on the Rue Jacob in Paris rather than at Versailles, since Britain refused to negotiate there with its former colonies as equals. The new republic's boundary ran west to the Mississippi, north to roughly today's Canadian line and south to Florida, which Britain handed back to Spain in a separate agreement.

American fishermen kept access to the waters off Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, and both nations were promised free navigation of the Mississippi. Congress agreed only to recommend that states return confiscated property to Loyalists, a clause most states simply ignored. British creditors were promised repayment of prewar debts, a provision that proved just as hard to enforce once the war was over.

France gave up nearly all of its North American mainland claims in 1763, ceding Canada and the land east of the Mississippi to Britain outright. West of the river, Louisiana had already gone to Spain in a separate, secret handover the year before, so France left the continent with almost nothing.

Britain gave some of it back elsewhere: it returned Guadeloupe, Martinique and Saint Lucia to France, and Havana and Manila, both seized during the war, to Spain. Britain kept Canada and Florida rather than the Caribbean sugar islands, a choice that looked odd to contemporaries who valued sugar revenue over cold farmland.

Delegates signed the treaty in Rome's Palazzo dei Conservatori on 25 March 1957. Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands were the six governments involved, the same six that had already pooled their coal and steel industries earlier in the decade. The treaty took effect on the first day of 1958.

What it created was a common market rather than a currency or a parliament with real teeth: internal tariffs would fall over a transition period and a shared external tariff would rise in their place. That body, the European Economic Community, absorbed Euratom's founding treaty on the same day and later grew into the European Union, expanding well beyond its original six members.

Nobody at Ryswick expected the peace to hold. The 1697 settlement closing the Nine Years' War mostly put Europe back where it had stood before the fighting started: France handed back Lorraine, Freiburg and Breisach, and pulled its troops out of Catalonia and several towns in the Spanish Netherlands, while keeping Strasbourg.

Louis XIV also recognised William III as King of England, dropped his support for the exiled Stuart claimant, and gave up rival claims on two German electorates. Both sides treated the deal as a pause rather than a resolution, watching the childless King Charles II of Spain, and war over his succession broke out again within three years of his death in 1700.

Rollo's Viking followers had already occupied land around Rouen for over a decade when Charles the Simple agreed in 911 to formally grant him the territory west of the Epte, in exchange for baptism and an oath to guard the Seine against further raids. Rollo took the Christian name Robert after his godfather at the ceremony.

The treaty was sealed with a betrothal between Rollo and Charles's young daughter Gisela. Rollo divided the land between the Epte and Risle among his own chieftains and made Rouen his capital, and his descendants pushed the borders further over the following century, building the duchy that eventually produced William the Conqueror.

The line agreed at Tordesillas ran 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands, roughly 2,100 kilometres of open Atlantic with almost nothing charted on either side of it. Everything discovered to the east went to Portugal, everything to the west to Castile, drawn up by Ferdinand and Isabella and John II of Portugal without asking Pope Alexander VI, whose earlier bulls it quietly overrode.

Nobody else in Europe felt bound by it. France's king Francis I is said to have asked to see the clause in Adam's will that excluded him from the world, and England and the Dutch, being Protestant, saw no reason to honour a line brokered by the Pope between two Catholic crowns. It took Julius II until 1506 to bless the treaty at all.

The treaties signed at Utrecht in 1713 let Philip V keep the Spanish throne on one condition: he and his heirs gave up any claim to France, and French princes gave up any claim to Spain, so the same king could never rule both. That single renunciation was the point the other terms were built around.

Britain came away the best paid party in the room. Spain ceded Gibraltar and Menorca, France handed over Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and Hudson Bay territory in North America, and Britain won a thirty-year contract, the asiento, to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish American colonies, a monopoly France had held until then.

Three brothers spent three years fighting each other before agreeing to stop. Lothair, Louis and Charles, all grandsons of Charlemagne, had already gone to war over their father Louis the Pious's uneven attempts to divide the inheritance, and only after Lothair's defeat at Fontenoy in 841 did the brothers sit down to settle it in 843.

The line they drew ran a middle kingdom, Lothair's Francia Media, between an eastern realm for Louis and a western one for Charles. The middle strip did not last: it splintered within a generation, while the eastern and western portions held together long enough to become the rough outlines of Germany and France.

At Waitangi in the Bay of Islands on 6 February 1840, around forty Maori chiefs put their names or marks to an agreement with the British Crown, with more signing at further sites over the following months. The document exists in two texts, English and Maori, drafted in haste and not identical in meaning.

Where the English version ceded the chiefs' sovereignty outright, the Maori text spoke of kawanatanga, closer to governance than sovereignty, while a promise of continued rangatiratanga over land and possessions left chiefs believing they retained authority the English wording did not grant them. That gap between the two texts has shaped New Zealand law and politics ever since.

Guthrum came to terms with Alfred only after losing a battle, not a war of attrition. His Viking army had chased Alfred into hiding in the Somerset marshes over the winter of 878, but Alfred's forces defeated Guthrum decisively at Ethandun that spring, and the peace struck afterward, remembered as the Treaty of Wedmore, was Guthrum's price for keeping his life.

Its terms were narrower than later legend suggests: Guthrum agreed to be baptised, taking Alfred as his godfather, and to withdraw his army from Wessex. The formal border between English and Viking-held territory, the line that created the Danelaw, was settled separately in a later, written agreement between the two leaders.

Italy signed on 20 May 1882 chiefly out of anger at France, which had just taken Tunisia, territory Italy had wanted for itself. Germany and Austria-Hungary already had a defensive pact of their own and extended it to include Italy, promising to back Rome if France attacked first, while Italy pledged neutrality if Russia moved against Vienna.

The alliance was renewed every few years into the twentieth century, but it depended on Austria-Hungary being the one attacked, not the aggressor. When Vienna itself opened hostilities in 1914, Italy declared neutrality and, the following year, joined the opposing side instead, ending its part in the pact for good.

No single document created the Triple Entente. It grew from three separate deals: a Franco-Russian alliance from 1894, the Anglo-French Entente Cordiale of 1904, and the 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention, which settled British and Russian rivalry over Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet by dividing Persia into zones of influence.

A British official, Eyre Crowe, called the resulting arrangement between the three powers little more than a shared frame of mind rather than a binding pact, and it carried no mutual defence obligation. That looseness let Britain weigh its own response independently in 1914, even though France, Russia and Britain all ended up fighting the Central Powers together.

Britain told Washington in early 1947 that it could no longer afford to keep funding the Greek government against communist insurgents or prop up Turkey, and it wanted the United States to take over within weeks. Truman addressed Congress on 12 March 1947 with an eighteen-minute speech committing American support to any nation resisting armed minorities or outside pressure, a pledge aimed squarely at Athens and Ankara but framed as universal.

Congress approved four hundred million dollars in aid that May, funding the Greek army in a civil war against insurgents partly backed by Yugoslavia. Secretary of State Dean Acheson had pressed sceptical lawmakers by warning that a communist Greece could spread like a rotten apple through the rest of the barrel, an image that reportedly did more to win votes than the speech itself.

Chief Justice John Roberts administered the oath at noon on 20 January 2017, on the Capitol's West Front, with Trump's hand on two Bibles: his own and Abraham Lincoln's. His inaugural address ran to just over sixteen minutes and warned of what he called American carnage, describing rusted factories and crime rates that fact checkers found did not match the figures of the time.

The crowd that gathered on the National Mall became its own dispute. Photographs comparing it unfavourably with Barack Obama's 2009 inauguration led the new press secretary to insist, incorrectly, that it had been the largest audience ever to witness an inauguration. Independent estimates put attendance at somewhere between 300,000 and 600,000.

On the morning of 30 June 1908, an object entering the atmosphere over the Podkamennaya Tunguska river in Siberia detonated several miles above the ground with a force estimated at anywhere from three to thirty megatons. It flattened roughly 2,150 square kilometres of forest in a butterfly-shaped pattern radiating from the point below the blast, yet left no crater at all.

The region was so remote that the only recorded deaths, up to three, are uncertain, and no scientific expedition reached the site for over a decade. The mineralogist Leonid Kulik led the first survey in 1921 and a fuller expedition in 1927, and found flattened trees but no meteorite fragments. The leading explanation remains an airburst from a stony asteroid some fifty to sixty metres across, though a comet fragment has also been proposed.

Habib Bourguiba spent years in French prisons and exile before the protocol that ended the protectorate was signed on 20 March 1956, between Grand Vizier Tahar Ben Ammar and France's foreign minister. Bourguiba treated the document as full independence and refused to negotiate further terms, becoming the country's first prime minister after elections held that April.

Independence did not mean France left entirely. French forces stayed at the naval base of Bizerte and in the south for years afterward, citing the war it was still fighting in neighbouring Algeria, and the base was not handed over until 1963, a lingering friction that formal treaties had not settled.

Bumin proclaimed himself Illig Qaghan at Otuken in 552, then died within months of doing it. His new title outlived him: his successors held the steppe empire he had founded together and kept expanding it, ruling it from twin capitals, Otuken in Mongolia and Suyab far to the west in the Chu valley.

At its widest reach the khaganate ran roughly six million square kilometres from Manchuria to the Black Sea, the first empire to span the steppe on that scale. It bordered both the Byzantine and Sassanid empires, and its protection is part of what let Sogdian merchant caravans keep moving safely across so much of Central Asia.

The school existed because of a vote-trading deal. In 1880, former Confederate colonel Wilbur Foster wanted the Black electorate of Macon County, Alabama, and Black leader Lewis Adams wanted a school; Adams agreed to deliver votes if Foster, once elected, secured state funding for one. Foster won, kept his word, and on 4 July 1881 classes opened in a borrowed shanty next to a church.

Booker T. Washington, aged twenty-five, arrived to run it with no campus at all. Within a year he had bought a former plantation of about a hundred acres, and students built the first permanent buildings themselves as part of their coursework, making bricks and laying walls while they studied. The institute grew to nearly 2,300 acres by the early twentieth century, still largely built by the people who studied there.

Before 450 BCE, Roman law lived in the memories of patrician priests, who could tell plebeians whatever they liked and call it tradition. Plebeians pushed back the one way that worked: secessio, walking out of the city en masse and leaving Rome without its labourers and soldiers until the Senate agreed to write the law down.

A board of ten men, the decemviri, drafted ten tables in 450 BCE and two more the following year, reportedly after sending someone to study Greek law codes first. The finished text was cast in bronze and set up in the Forum where anyone could read it. Much of the content covered everyday disputes, debt, property, family, but the act of posting it at all was the point: the law could no longer be whatever a patrician said it was that day.

American officials assumed the U-2 flew too high to be hit, and when contact was lost with pilot Francis Gary Powers on 1 May 1960, Washington issued a cover story about a weather plane that had strayed off course over Turkey. Nikita Khrushchev let the lie stand for days before revealing that Powers had survived and was in Soviet custody, along with the spy plane's camera equipment.

Eisenhower broke with the usual practice of denial and admitted responsibility for the overflight programme on 11 May, days before a long-planned four power summit in Paris. Khrushchev walked out on the second day after Eisenhower refused to apologise, ending the brief warming in relations that diplomats had called the Spirit of Camp David.

French president Charles de Gaulle blocked British applications to join the Common Market twice, in 1963 and again in 1967, distrusting a country he thought would always side with Washington and whose efficient farms threatened France's protected agricultural policy. Only after de Gaulle left office in 1969 did the other five members reopen the question.

Prime Minister Edward Heath signed the Treaty of Accession in January 1972, Parliament passed the European Communities Act that October, and British membership took effect on 1 January 1973 alongside Ireland and Denmark. By then British exporters were already selling more to Western Europe than to the Commonwealth, which had done as much as any treaty to change London's calculation.

Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan did not inherit the caliphate so much as outlast his rivals for it. As governor of Syria, he refused to accept Ali as caliph after the murder of Uthman, and years of civil war between their factions, the First Fitna, ended only when Ali was assassinated in 661 and Mu'awiya's forces held the field.

He moved the capital and treasury from Medina to Damascus, his own long-held power base, turning what had been an Arabian institution into one governed from a Roman-Byzantine city. He also broke with precedent by naming his own son as successor, making the caliphate hereditary for the first time.

The main evidence for Narmer's unification of the two Egyptian kingdoms is a single carved slab of siltstone, found at Hierakonpolis and known as the Narmer Palette. On one face he wears the crown of Upper Egypt; on the other, the crown of Lower Egypt. Many Egyptologists identify him with Menes, whom the later priest Manetho named as the first king of a unified Egypt, though the two names are never linked in a contemporary source.

A year label of Narmer's, found at Abydos in 1993, appears to record the same event shown on the palette, suggesting it depicts an actual campaign rather than pure symbolism. His name has turned up at some 98 sites across Egypt and into Canaan and the Sinai, far more widely than any king before him, marking a jump in the reach of a single ruler around 3100 BC.

Queen Margaret I of Denmark built the Union of Kalmar around a boy who was not her son. Eric of Pomerania, her adopted great nephew, had no personal claim strong enough to unite three kingdoms on his own, so it was Margaret's own standing as regent of Denmark, Norway and already much of Sweden that made his coronation at Kalmar on 17 June 1397 possible.

The three crowns stayed nominally joined for over a century, but Denmark was never quite strong enough to hold Norway and Sweden inside it against their own nobles' wishes. Resentment of Danish dominance ran especially deep in Sweden, and after the Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520 a rebellion led by Gustav Vasa broke the union for good when he was elected King of Sweden in 1523.

The Union of Krewo was a marriage contract before it was anything else. Jogaila, Grand Duke of Lithuania, agreed to marry the young Queen Jadwiga of Poland, and to pay 200,000 florins to buy her out of an existing engagement to a Habsburg duke. In return he became King of Poland the following year, ruling by right of his wife rather than by his own crown.

The price was religious. Jogaila had to convert from paganism to Catholicism and take the baptismal name Wladyslaw, then bring the Lithuanian nobility with him and free tens of thousands of Polish captives held from earlier wars. The union bound two states that had spent generations fighting each other into a partnership that, through later treaties, lasted for four centuries.

Cape Colony, Natal, Transvaal and the Orange River Colony had spent the previous decade at war with each other or under separate administrations before uniting on 31 May 1910. Louis Botha, a former Boer general who had fought the British eight years earlier, became the new dominion's first prime minister, heading a government built around reconciling the two white settler communities.

That reconciliation left almost everyone else out of it. The Cape's old franchise, which had let some Black and mixed-race men vote regardless of race, survived only in the Cape province and was steadily hemmed in, while a national Native Affairs department was created to administer segregation across the whole union from the start.

Signed on 23 January 1579, the Union bound Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht and Groningen together on shared defence, taxation and, unusually for the time, a promise of personal freedom of religion. It answered the Union of Arras, signed weeks earlier, in which the southern provinces had reaffirmed their loyalty to Philip II and split the Low Countries along a line still visible in the Belgian-Dutch border.

More provinces joined through 1579 and 1580, among them Ghent, Antwerp and Brussels, though Upper Guelders never signed at all. The agreement made no claim to independence itself, but it gave the northern provinces a shared structure to govern themselves with, one historians treat as the working foundation of the republic they later became.

Delegates from fifty governments met in San Francisco starting 25 April 1945, while fighting in Europe was still going on, to turn the wartime alliance into a permanent body. Two months of drafting produced a charter signed on 26 June 1945; Poland, absent from the conference, added its signature later and is still counted among the founding members.

The charter took legal effect on 24 October 1945 once the five states meant to hold permanent Security Council seats, along with a majority of the other signatories, had ratified it. That date is marked each year as United Nations Day, distinct from the June signing that most accounts point to as the founding moment.

The territory had already changed hands twice, annexed by Brazil in 1821 after being fought over by Spain and Argentina. In 1825 a small band calling itself the Thirty Three Orientals, led by Juan Antonio Lavalleja, declared it independent again with Argentine backing, setting off a war between Argentina and Brazil that dragged on for over a year without a winner.

It was a British diplomat, Viscount Ponsonby, who broke the deadlock. Neither Buenos Aires nor Rio de Janeiro trusted the other with the territory, so the 1828 Treaty of Montevideo split the difference: an independent Uruguay that neither empire controlled, a solution that suited British trading interests in the region as much as anyone else's.

An annexation treaty McKinley signed in 1897 could not muster the two-thirds Senate majority a treaty required, so supporters instead pushed the Newlands Resolution, which needed only simple majorities in both chambers. It passed the House in June 1898 and the Senate that July, and McKinley signed it days later. Queen Liliuokalani, deposed from her throne in 1893, protested the move to the end.

The timing mattered: with the Spanish-American War underway that spring, Hawaii's value as a mid-ocean naval stopover weakened opposition in Congress considerably. A petition against annexation gathered signatures from more than half of the roughly 39,000 native Hawaiians then living, and no popular vote in Hawaii was ever held. The formal transfer ceremony took place in Honolulu that August.

A bomb tore through a West Berlin discotheque on 5 April 1986, killing three people including two American servicemen. Washington blamed Libyan agents, and ten days later F-111s and carrier aircraft struck targets in Tripoli and Benghazi in Operation El Dorado Canyon, aimed in part at Muammar Gaddafi's own compound at Bab al-Azizia.

Gaddafi survived, reportedly warned in advance by Malta's prime minister and out of the residence before the bombs landed. He declared the raid a victory over the United States and renamed the country the Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya soon after. Libyan officials said dozens of people were killed in the strikes, among them, by Gaddafi's disputed account, an adopted infant daughter.

A Chinese fighter pilot had made a habit of flying dangerously close to American reconnaissance flights off Hainan Island, and on 1 April 2001 one of those passes went wrong. His J-8 clipped a US Navy EP-3, broke apart, and he was never found. The crippled American plane, its nose smashed and an engine damaged, made an unauthorised emergency landing on Chinese soil.

China held the 24 American crew members for eleven days and demanded an apology Washington was unwilling to give outright. The standoff broke when the United States sent a letter saying it was very sorry for the pilot's death and for landing without permission, wording vague enough for both governments to call it a resolution. China released the crew and returned the aircraft in pieces.

Nine states had to say yes before the document drafted in Philadelphia could take effect, and nobody was certain they would. Delaware ratified first, in December 1787. New Hampshire became the ninth in June 1788, clearing the threshold, though the outcome had been anything but settled in several state conventions where the vote was close and bitterly argued.

New York and Virginia, whose support the new government badly needed, ratified only after Federalist writers, chiefly Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay, published a long series of newspaper essays defending the plan. Both states came around only once opponents were promised that a bill of rights would follow. It did, four years later.

The treaty signed in Washington on 19 January 1960 replaced a 1951 security pact that Japan had accepted as the price of ending American occupation. The new version added mutual defence obligations and required Washington to consult Tokyo before moving forces, terms the original had not bothered to include.

Ratifying it back in Japan proved far harder than negotiating it. Prime Minister Nobusuke Kishi forced a vote through parliament after having police carry out Socialist lawmakers who tried to block it, and the manoeuvre triggered some of the largest protests in Japan's postwar history. A Tokyo University student, Michiko Kanba, died in clashes near parliament on 15 June, days before the treaty took effect.

Franklin Roosevelt's Executive Order 6102, signed on 5 April 1933, ordered Americans to hand in their gold coin, bullion and certificates to a Federal Reserve bank by the start of May, in exchange for a fixed 20.67 dollars an ounce. Anyone keeping more than 100 dollars worth of gold risked fines or prison.

Weeks later Roosevelt raised the official gold price to 35 dollars an ounce, cutting the dollar's gold value by about forty percent overnight and letting the government pump more money into a deflating economy. The Gold Reserve Act the following year completed the break, and private citizens could not legally own gold bullion again until 1974.

No sitting American president had ever met a leader of North Korea when Trump and Kim Jong Un sat down at the Capella Resort on Sentosa Island, Singapore, on 12 June 2018. The two had traded insults and nuclear threats the previous year, Trump mocking Kim as Rocket Man, before a sudden thaw brought them to the same table.

They signed a brief joint statement promising new relations, security guarantees for the North, the recovery of war remains, and denuclearisation of the peninsula, without setting out how or by when. North Korea had earlier listed conditions of its own, including an end to joint military exercises. The specifics were left to officials to negotiate afterwards, and progress soon stalled.

The Afghan government that American and allied forces had propped up for two decades collapsed in days. The Taliban entered Kabul on 15 August 2021 almost without a fight, and the president fled the country, leaving thousands of Afghans who had worked with foreign forces to scramble towards the airport for evacuation flights.

A suicide bombing at the airport's Abbey Gate on 26 August killed thirteen American service members and well over a hundred Afghans in the crowd. The last American military flight left just before midnight on 30 August, ending the war, though an unknown number of American citizens and Afghan visa holders were left unable to leave in time.

Four republics signed the treaty of union on 30 December 1922: Russia, Ukraine, Byelorussia and the Transcaucasian Federation, which then covered Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan together. Mikhail Kalinin led the Russian delegation, and the document was ratified the next day by the first Congress of Soviets.

The new union kept the outward form of a federation of sovereign states, each with its own government and, on paper, a right to secede. In practice power ran through the Communist Party rather than through those republican structures, and further republics joined the union over the following decades as Soviet borders shifted.

For nearly sixty years, popes had refused to leave the Vatican grounds, calling themselves prisoners after Italian troops seized Rome and the last Papal States in 1870. The dispute, known as the Roman Question, left the papacy without any territory of its own to guarantee it independence from the Italian government.

Benito Mussolini and Cardinal Pietro Gasparri signed the Lateran Treaty on 11 February 1929, ending the standoff by creating Vatican City as a sovereign state under the Pope, with Italy paying compensation for the confiscated lands. The tiny enclave, barely half a square kilometre, remains the world's smallest independent state.

Students marched in Prague on 17 November 1989 to mark the fiftieth anniversary of Nazi violence against Czech students, and police beat the demonstrators. A rumour spread soon after, amplified by Radio Free Europe, that one student named Martin Smid had been killed. He had not, but the false report brought far larger crowds onto the streets over the following days than the original march had drawn.

A general strike on 27 November convinced the Communist Party its position was finished, and it gave up power within days. Alexander Dubcek, sidelined since the Soviet crushing of the Prague Spring two decades earlier, was elected speaker of parliament on 28 December. Vaclav Havel, the playwright who had led the dissident group Civic Forum, became president the next day, on 29 December 1989.

Congress met in Caracas on 5 July 1811, and seven of the ten provinces of the old Captaincy General voted to break with Spain. Francisco de Miranda, an ageing veteran of the French Revolution, and the young Simon Bolivar were among those pushing the delegates past their hesitation.

The republic barely survived a year. An earthquake struck republican territory in March 1812, which royalist clergy called divine punishment, and Domingo de Monteverde's forces then pressed the advantage. Miranda signed an armistice that July, and Bolivar would spend over a decade fighting to reclaim what the declaration had promised.

Khmer Rouge units had been raiding across the border for two years, and in April 1978 killed over 3,000 people at Ba Chuc. Hanoi answered on 25 December 1978 with a full invasion of the country it viewed as a Chinese proxy on its border. Phnom Penh fell within two weeks and the Khmer Rouge army lost roughly half its strength.

Vietnam installed the People's Republic of Kampuchea under Heng Samrin on 8 January 1979, ending the genocide but not the war. Pol Pot's forces retreated to camps in Thailand and kept fighting, and most of the world refused to recognise the new government, letting the ousted Khmer Rouge keep Cambodia's seat at the United Nations. Vietnamese troops stayed for a decade, withdrawing only in 1989.

The first shots, at a dormitory just after 7 a.m. on 16 April 2007, killed two students and were initially treated by campus police as an isolated domestic incident. Classes continued for more than two hours while Seung-Hui Cho, a 23-year-old senior, mailed a package of writings and video to a television network before returning to campus with two pistols and chains.

At Norris Hall he chained the main doors shut from the inside, then moved between classrooms firing on students and faculty for roughly nine minutes before killing himself as police broke in. Thirty people died in that building alone, thirty-two in total, in what remains the deadliest campus shooting in United States history.

The treaty Rome struck with the Visigoths in 418 covered land around Toulouse, not Spain. Iberia came later and by conquest rather than grant, as Visigothic kings pushed south and west across the peninsula through the fifth century while the Western Roman state that had once hosted them collapsed.

By the time Rome's authority in the west ended in 476, the Visigoths already held most of what Rome had once promised them on paper, and more besides. Their capital shifted from Toulouse to Toledo by the mid sixth century, marking Iberia rather than Gaul as the kingdom's lasting home.

On 7 March 1965, state troopers attacked civil rights marchers crossing the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, with tear gas and clubs. Televised images of the assault, later called Bloody Sunday, pushed Congress toward action that had stalled for years despite the Fifteenth Amendment's fifty-year-old promise.

President Lyndon Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act on 6 August 1965. It outlawed literacy tests and similar devices used to disqualify Black voters, and it required jurisdictions with a documented history of discrimination to clear any change to voting rules with federal officials before enacting it.

Excommunicated and facing German princes ready to depose him, Henry IV crossed the Alps at Mont Cenis in the depths of winter, travelling with his wife Bertha and their young son, to reach Pope Gregory VII at Canossa Castle in January 1077. He is said to have worn a monk's hair shirt and gone barefoot in the snow, then waited outside the gate rather than be turned away.

He stayed there three days before Gregory let him in, absolved him, and shared communion with him that evening. The reconciliation was personal rather than political: Gregory restored Henry to the Church but not to unquestioned authority over his rebellious nobles, and within a few years the two men were at war again, ending in a second excommunication.

Historians usually date the Warring States period's start to 475 BC, the year the Spring and Autumn period is conventionally said to end, though ancient writers themselves disagreed on the boundary. Seven states, Qin, Qi, Chu, Yan and the three successor states of Jin, spent the next two and a half centuries fighting over what was left of Zhou China.

War pushed change faster than peace had: chariots gave way to massed infantry armed with crossbows and iron swords, and Zhao fielded China's first cavalry unit in 307 BC. The same pressure produced rival schools of thought, Legalism, Confucianism, Daoism and Mohism among them, each offering rulers a different theory of how to survive.

Moscow signed the treaty on 14 May 1955, five days after West Germany formally joined NATO. Seven other governments put their names to it alongside the Soviet Union: Albania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Hungary, Poland and Romania. The stated purpose was collective security in Europe, but the timing tied it directly to West German rearmament.

In practice the pact's forces were used against its own members more often than against NATO. Soviet-led troops crushed the Hungarian uprising in 1956 and, under the pact's banner, invaded Czechoslovakia in 1968 to end the Prague Spring. Albania withdrew in 1968 in protest at that invasion, and the alliance itself dissolved in 1991 as Soviet control over Eastern Europe collapsed.

Five countries, the United States, Britain, Japan, France and Italy, agreed in 1922 to hold their battleship tonnage to a fixed ratio near 5:5:3:1.75:1.75, letting the US and Britain each keep 525,000 tons of capital ships while Japan was held to 315,000. Individual battleships were capped at 35,000 tons and guns no larger than 16 inches.

Cruisers, destroyers and submarines were left uncapped in number, only in size, at 10,000 tons apiece, a gap navies spent the following decade exploiting. Japan resented a ratio that ranked it below Britain and the United States, and the treaty's limits held only until the 1930s, when Japan withdrew from them.

Five men were arrested inside the Democratic National Committee's offices in Washington's Watergate complex in the early hours of 17 June 1972, sent there by former CIA officer E. Howard Hunt and ex FBI agent G. Gordon Liddy to photograph documents and fit hidden microphones on staff telephones. A security guard, Frank Wills, found tape holding a door latch open and called the police rather than assuming a cleaner had left it there.
