One of the burglars, James McCord, had taped the doors horizontally, leaving tape visible along the edges where an earlier attempt had already been cleaned up. That small carelessness brought an unmarked police car to the scene within minutes, and the five men were caught hiding behind a partition and arrested under false names.

James Watt wanted his engine to turn a wheel rather than merely pump water, and a rival held the patent on the obvious solution, the crank. His employee William Murdoch proposed a workaround: a sun and planet gear, in which a gear fixed to the piston rod orbited one on the output shaft, converting the piston's push and pull into continuous rotation.

Watt patented the mechanism in 1781. Freed from the crank, the engine could now stand anywhere, not only beside a river turning a waterwheel, and factories began locating themselves near labour and transport instead of a fall of water. That relocation, more than the engine itself, reshaped where industry in Britain grew.

Bill Clinton had campaigned in 1992 on a promise to end welfare as people knew it, and on 22 August 1996 he signed a bill that did exactly that against the objections of several of his own aides, three of whom resigned over it. It abolished Aid to Families with Dependent Children, the open-ended entitlement that had run since 1935, and replaced it with block grants to the states called Temporary Assistance for Needy Families.

The new system capped federal benefits at five years over a recipient's lifetime and required most adults to start working within two years of receiving aid. Caseloads fell by more than half between 1997 and 2000, a drop supporters credited to the new incentives and critics attributed partly to a strong economy and stricter eligibility.

The new agency absorbed duties from a scattering of earlier bodies: the International Sanitary Conferences held on and off since 1851, the Pan American Sanitary Bureau of 1902, the Paris-based Office International d'Hygiene Publique of 1907, and the League of Nations health organisation. Its constitution came into force on 7 April 1948, a date still marked as World Health Day, though it did not begin operating until that September.

One of its earliest priorities was a mass vaccination and treatment campaign against yaws, meant to show that a single coordinating agency could do more than a patchwork of colonial and national health offices ever had. Membership was open to any UN member state and, unusually, to non-members admitted by a simple majority vote of the health assembly.

The first 220 cables appeared on 28 November 2010, a heavily redacted trickle from an archive that would eventually reach 251,287 documents. The source was Chelsea Manning, an army intelligence analyst stationed in Iraq, who was later convicted and sentenced to thirty-five years before President Obama commuted her sentence in 2017.

WikiLeaks did not simply post the files. It handed them first to five newspapers, including Le Monde, Der Spiegel, The Guardian and The New York Times, who jointly reviewed and redacted material to protect named informants before publishing selected cables themselves. The full unredacted set was not public until September 2011, after a security lapse exposed the encryption password.

Wikipedia began as a side project to fix a bottleneck. Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger were building Nupedia, an online encyclopedia written by credentialed experts and slowed to a crawl by peer review; only a couple of dozen articles had cleared the process in a year. On 15 January 2001 they launched a wiki as a faster feeder for drafts.

Anyone could edit a page and see the change appear instantly, and within a month the feeder had outpaced the project it was meant to feed. Nupedia was quietly shut down in 2003, while the wiki kept its earlier name and grew into an encyclopedia written almost entirely by unpaid volunteers.

Tennessee's ratification on 18 August 1920 was the 36th needed to put the amendment into the Constitution, and it came down to one vote. Harry Burn, a 24 year old state representative who had opposed ratification, switched sides on the floor after his mother mailed him a note telling him to vote for suffrage.

Opponents tried to stop a final quorum by fleeing across the state line to Decatur, Alabama, but the tally already stood. A suffragist in the chamber rang a small Liberty Bell replica when the result was confirmed, and the amendment was certified on 26 August 1920.

Chicago beat out New York, Washington and St Louis for the right to mark four hundred years since Columbus reached the Americas, and it built an entire temporary city in Jackson Park to do it. Frederick Law Olmsted laid out the grounds and Daniel Burnham directed the construction of the so-called White City, a cluster of Beaux-Arts exhibition halls coated in white stucco meant to look like marble.

The fair's board resisted the idea of a giant wheel until construction ran late into the spring, leaving George Ferris little time to finish his design of thirty-six cars, each able to carry forty people, rising 264 feet above the fairgrounds. Once it opened it drew crowds large enough to pull the exposition itself back from the edge of a financial loss.

The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade had governed world trade since 1948 without ever becoming a formal institution, running instead as a series of rounds of negotiation among contracting parties. Ministers meeting in Marrakesh in April 1994 signed an agreement to replace it with a standing body, and the World Trade Organization opened for business on 1 January 1995.

Unlike GATT, the WTO could enforce its own rulings through a binding dispute settlement system and covered services and intellectual property as well as goods. Its membership grew from the roughly 120 governments present at Marrakesh to more than 160, each bound by the same set of agreed rules on tariffs and trade practice.

Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin spent eight days in February 1945 at palaces on the Crimean coast near Yalta, meeting while Soviet troops were already inside Germany. They agreed to split Germany and Berlin into occupation zones, with France given a zone carved from the American and British shares, and to move Poland's eastern border to the Curzon Line while compensating Poland with German territory in the west.

Stalin promised to enter the war against Japan within three months of Germany's surrender, in exchange for territory including South Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, and agreed the Soviet Union would join the new United Nations with a Security Council veto. The three also signed a declaration promising free elections across liberated Europe, a promise Stalin did not keep in the territories his army occupied.

The high visibility vest that every French driver keeps in the car became the protest's uniform after a planned rise in diesel tax pushed motorists, mostly from small towns and rural areas outside Paris, onto roundabouts and motorway toll booths from November 2018. More than 300,000 people turned out on the first weekend alone, with no political party or union behind them.

The demands widened fast, into a list of 42 covering wages, pensions and a form of direct democracy by referendum. Facing weekly clashes on the Champs-Elysees, President Macron scrapped the fuel tax rise, raised the minimum wage by 100 euros a month and cut taxes on overtime pay. Roughly three million people took part before the movement wound down through 2019.

Painter George Catlin had floated the idea of a protected wilderness decades earlier, but it took an act of Congress and Ulysses Grant's signature on 1 March 1872 to create one. Yellowstone became the first tract of land anywhere set aside by a national government purely for public enjoyment.

The law described it plainly as a public park and pleasuring ground, closed to settlement and reserved for its geysers, canyons and wildlife. Other countries followed the model within a few decades, and national park systems now cover land on every inhabited continent.

Officers of the Committee of Union and Progress had spent years organising in secret against three decades of autocratic rule under Sultan Abdulhamid II. In July 1908, Major Ahmed Niyazi took to the hills near Resne with a band of soldiers rather than face arrest, and other units across Ottoman Macedonia followed, threatening to march on the capital if the constitution was not restored.

Facing a mutiny he could not suppress, Abdulhamid issued a decree on 24 July reinstating the 1876 constitution and recalling a parliament that had been suspended for thirty years. Enver Bey, one of the officers behind the revolt, was celebrated in Ottoman newspapers as a hero of liberty. The sultan kept his throne for another year before the same movement deposed him in 1909.

King Wu of Zhou crossed the Yellow River around 1046 BC with an army said to number 45,000 men and 300 chariots, backed by his ally Jiang Ziya, and met the last Shang king's forces at Muye. The Shang army broke, the king reportedly burned himself to death in his palace, and Wu declared that the Shang had lost the mandate of heaven, a claim later dynasties reused to justify overthrowing the one before.

The dynasty that followed lasted longer than any other in Chinese history, roughly 790 years down to 256 BC, though for the last few centuries its kings held little more than ceremonial authority while rival states fought for control. Zhou rule is usually split at 771 BC into a Western and an Eastern period, the second dominated by the regional lords the earlier Zhou kings had enfeoffed.

Ian Smith's government had declared independence from Britain unilaterally in 1965 rather than accept majority rule, and fought a guerrilla war for fifteen years to keep it that way. The war ended not on a battlefield but at a London conference: the Lancaster House Agreement of December 1979 put the territory back under British authority as a colony, on paper, just long enough to hold elections it could not otherwise have held.

Robert Mugabe's Zimbabwe African National Union won those elections outright in early 1980. The country became independent Zimbabwe, with international recognition this time, on 18 April 1980, and Mugabe, previously ZANU's general secretary, became its first leader. Fifteen years of white minority rule under Smith were over.

British codebreakers in Room 40 intercepted a coded cable from Germany's foreign secretary, Arthur Zimmermann, to his ambassador in Mexico and had it substantially decrypted within a day, though refining it took weeks. It proposed a wartime alliance in which Mexico would recover Texas, New Mexico and Arizona if the United States entered the war against Germany, with Japan invited to join as well.

Washington received the decoded text on 24 February 1917 and made it public a week later. Zimmermann himself confirmed at a press conference on 3 March that the telegram was genuine, removing any doubt it was a British fabrication and pushing American public opinion sharply toward the war Germany was trying to keep it out of.

Prussia had abolished its own internal tolls in 1818 and spent the following years inviting neighbouring states to do the same, a project that finally became a single customs union on 1 January 1834. Bavaria, Wurttemberg, Baden and a string of smaller states joined, and goods could cross what had been dozens of separate tariff lines without a fresh toll at every border.

Austria was pointedly left out, and not by accident. Vienna's economy was heavily protected, and Metternich would not split the Austrian empire's own vast customs territory to fit inside a German union led by his rival. That exclusion left Prussia, not Austria, running the economic framework that German unification would later be built on.
